results.description: # Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure. For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill⁠(opens in a new window) to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply. ... Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare. ... For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages: - Validate and fix the upstream vulnerability. The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability. - Give affected organizations time to act. results.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence が PHP2Shell の脆弱性公開前の悪用を MadPot で特定 | Amazon Web Services
results.description:
本ブログは 2026 年 10 月 21 日に公開された AWS Blog “[Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot](//aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/)” を翻訳したものです。
Amazon Threat Intelligence は、MadPot のテレメトリから、2026 年 10 月 17 日に PHP2Shell の悪用の試みがあったことを特定しました。これは CVE-2026-109618 と CVE-2026-109619 が一般に公開される 4 日前のことです。この悪用の試みは、商用の匿名化ネットワークに関連する IP アドレスから行われていました。この脆弱性に関する情報がエンバーゴ (公開制限) の対象となっていた間に、匿名化された IP アドレスからハニーポットが標的にされました。このことから、このアクティビティは脅威アクターによるものと考えられます。ただし、このアクターが公開前にどのようにエクスプロイトの情報を入手したのかは、原文公開時点ではまだ不明でした。
PHP のエンバーゴは、2026 年 10 月 21 日 14:00 (UTC、日本時間同日 23:00) に解除される予定でした。解除当日、Amazon Threat Intelligence はこの脆弱性に対する複数の概念実証エクスプロイトを特定しました。最も早いものは 2026 年 10 月 21 日 2:00 (UTC、日本時間同日 11:00) ごろに確認されています。その後、2026 年 10 月 21 日 2:00 から 8:00 (UTC、日本時間同日 11:00 から 17:00) までの間にも、Amazon Threat Intelligence は、別の匿名化インフラストラクチャから MadPot を標的とした PHP2Shell の悪用の試みを新たに特定しました。実際のペイロードや使用された匿名化インフラストラクチャはそれぞれ異なっており、複数のアクターによるものであることが示唆されています。2026

results.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot | Amazon Web Services
results.description:
Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.
The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.
The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17th.

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.
## Immediate recommended actions
1. Upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project [released emergency fixes](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php) for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see [Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot](/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/).

Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles `multipart/form-data` request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses.

results.title: Security audit of PHP-SRC
Security review of PHP documentation
results.description:
Performing a security review of PHP documentation is therefore essential—not only to promote modern, secure development standards, but also to help protect applications and users from common vulnerabilities. To that end, the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund, Inc. and the PHP Foundation engaged with Quarkslab to perform a security audit of the code snippets in the English version of PHP documentation, focused on some specific pages. The PHP documentation (i.e., manual) consists primarily of a function reference, but also contains a language reference, explanations of some of PHP’s major features, and other supplemental information.

Scope of work The defined objectives for this collaboration were to perform a security review of the PHP documentation in order to have an overall assessment of the quality of the included code snippets. As the documentation is quite extensive, the scope was reduced based on priorities and the review was performed in a best-effort manner, within the allocated time frame of the review. Quarkslab based the review on the following priorities, as agreed with the OSTIF and PHP Foundation: Documentation code snippet review as first priorityFocus on specific topics, such as filesytem, then cryptography, and more if time permits/relevant  Then focus on user-comment code snippetsStarting with curl_setopt  Note: The security review report specifies all reviewed documentation pages for clarity purposes.  The security review was performed in 10 days. Findings During the time frame of the security audit, Quarkslab discovered several security issues and vulnerabilities. Given that the scope is focused on snippets of code and user comments, no severity ranking is provided. Overall, we have 81 observed issues. All details are provided in the report. Warning Since the scope focused on code examples, some issues (e.g., hardcoded secret keys) were not considered as such since their purpose is to illustrate the example. Following Quarkslab’s recommendations, the PHP foundation should have added disclaimers and notes on such practices.  Conclusion Initial review Quarkslab conducted a security assessment of several PHP documentation pages, with particular attention to user comments on the most heavily commented pages. The review revealed that code quality best practices were not consistently enforced (e.g., error handling and input validation), posing potential risks if snippets were copied into implementations; documentation for deprecated functions was not always updated; and user comments, especially older ones, should not be trusted by default given the project’s evolution After several months The PHP maintainers incorporated Quarkslab’s audit recommendations, resulting in improved overall quality of the PHP documentation. Quarkslab nevertheless recommends rendering the appendix introduced in pull request 4797 to further promote best practices in error handling and input validation. Note: Before this blogpost publication, PHP mainteners informed Quarkslab that the issue regarding the appendix had been resolved; Quarsklab did not verify this point but relied on the PHP maintainers’ assurance.  Quarkslab underlines the prompt responses from PHP Foundation team members to fix the observed issues in the documentation.

results.title: Exploiting Chamilo during a Red Team engagement
results.description:
During a Red Team engagement, we found ourselves in a situation where the scope associated with our client was extremely restricted. However, we identified the existence of an up-to-date instance of Chamilo exposed over the Internet. This CMS is developed in PHP, making it a particularly interesting target for us. Knowing that several vulnerabilities were identified in 2023 by fellow researchers from [RandoriSec](https://x.com/randorisec) and [STAR Labs](https://x.com/starlabs_sg), we were confident of our chances of finding new vulnerabilities that would allow us to obtain our initial access.
We performed a time-constrained source code audit and identified numerous vulnerabilities in the latest version of the CMS (1.11.26 at the time), although only a few were useful in building a complete exploitation chain that allowed us to perform a Remote Code Execution without authentication.
Based on our source code audit, we identified the following vulnerabilities:
- Multiple Arbitrary File Write to Remote Code Execution
- V1: Arbitrary File Write via /main/inc/ajax/document.ajax.php
- V2: Arbitrary File Write via /main/admin/user_edit.php
- Path Traversal to Local File Inclusion to Remote Code Execution
- V3: Path Traversal to Local File Inclusion via call to `require()` in /main/inc/ajax/plugin.ajax.php
- Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
- V4: SSRF via the HTML to PDF conversion feature
- Multiple Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
- Multiple Reflected Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
- V5: Reflected Cross Site Scripting (XSS) in /main/session/session_category_list.php
- V6: Reflected Cross Site Scripting (XSS) in /main/upload/index.php
- Multiple Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
- V7: Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS) in /main/calendar/agenda.php
- V8: Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS) via the messaging feature
> Static analysis (manual reading of the code) was used to identify all the vulnerabilities without any SAST tools or any other tooling.
Amongst the 8 vulnerabilities identified in the core, one (V1) was used in our chain to achieve RCE (optionally V3 could have been used), as it is described in the diagram below.

results.title: Pwn everything Bounce everywhere all at once (part 2)
results.description:
In this series of articles we describe how, during an "assumed breach" security audit, we compromised multiple web applications on our client's network to carry out a watering hole attack by installing fake Single Sign-On pages on compromised servers. In our second episode we take a look at SOPlanning, a project management application that we encountered during the audit.

SOPlanning is an open source web application written in PHP used for, you guess it... planning. It is widely used for online project management and many big companies with complex planning needs use it. This article covers vulnerabilities identified in the (at the time) latest version of [SOPlanning](https://www.soplanning.org) ([v1.52.02](https://sourceforge.net/projects/soplanning/files/soplanning/1.52.02/)). The following vulnerabilities were identified and reported to the vendor, then, fixed in version [v1.53.02](https://sourceforge.net/projects/soplanning/files/soplanning/1.53.02/):
### Vulnerabilities
- V0: Error Based SQL Injection (pre-auth)
- V1: Authentication Bypass (exploitable by chaining with V0)
- V2: Arbitrary File Delete (exploitable by chaining with V1)
- V3: Arbitrary File Upload to Remote Code Execution (exploitable by chaining with V2)
- V4: `ZipArchive::extractTo()` Race Condition to Remote Code Execution (exploitable by chaining with V1)
These vulnerabilities, despite being uncorrelated, can be chained together to create two exploitation chains leading to unauthenticated Remote Code Execution(RCE).

By auditing the code of the files www/planning_param.php and www/planning.php, we were able to identify the possibility of injecting ourselves into an SQL query. Indeed, variable `$_SESSION['filtreGroupeProjet']` is populated via the information stored in variable `$_COOKIE['filtreGroupeProjet']` (controllable by an attacker).

results.description: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability | Cloudflare Blog October 21, 2026 # Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability Daniele Molteni Dan Jones and Kuber Nandwani Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release. All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed `session.upload_progress.name` are not covered by the WAF rule. The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability. More information to follow. October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic. Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell. Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic. Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives. To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability. Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog. The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users. ... PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet. ... The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released. An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker. The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens: Vulnerability What goes wrong CVE-2026-109618 PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid. CVE-2026-109619 A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data. These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update. Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix. ... ## Copy link New rules For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). To analyze blocked requests, visit Security > Security Analytics > Events. Filter by the rule IDs in the table above and inspect the matched request, action, and path. Customers who need to tailor the protection can update the scope of the Managed Ruleset to the parts of an application where it is relevant. ... ## Copy link Update PHP and keep the protection enabled Cloudflare customers using our Managed Ruleset are protected by default. results.description: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF | Cloudflare Blog October 21, 2026 # Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF Daniele Molteni Elie Roudninski Nick Downie Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester. These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper. Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error. With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability. And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans. ... The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction. As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory: ``` GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini ``` Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence: ``` 200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET ``` Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker. ... we ... year ... Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform: Field cf.waf.signature.response.confidence Confidence values associated with matching signatures cf.waf.signature.response.categories Categories associated with matching signatures cf.waf.signature.response.ref Signature reference IDs, up to 10 The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded. We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule. ... Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response. Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules. We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections. ... You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path.
